title: Bent Track or Worn Rollers? Diagnosing a Jerky Garage Door
description: Garage door jumping, jerking, or jamming on the way up? Here's how to tell a bent track from worn rollers, what each repair involves, and what it costs.

h1: Bent Track or Worn Rollers? How to Diagnose a Garage Door That Jumps, Jerks, or Jams
intro: A door that jumps, jerks, or jams on the way up almost always points to one of two parts: the rollers riding inside the track, or the track itself. The trouble is they produce overlapping symptoms, so homeowners often guess wrong and either replace rollers that were fine or ignore a track problem that's about to get worse. Here's how to tell them apart before you call anyone, what each repair involves, and why letting one go usually damages the other.

sections.heading: Why these two get confused
sections.body: Rollers and track work as a pair — the rollers are the small wheels (nylon or steel) bolted to each panel, and the track is the vertical and curved steel channel they ride in. A problem with either one shows up as the same basic complaint: the door doesn't glide, it lurches. That's why "it jumps" or "it jerks" isn't enough information on its own. The fix is to watch and listen more carefully, because the two failure modes actually behave differently once you know what to look for.

sections.heading: Signs it's the rollers
sections.body:
Worn rollers tend to announce themselves with sound and a repeating rhythm rather than a single catch point:

- **A steady grinding, squeaking, or clicking** that happens on every single rotation of the roller, not just once per cycle.
- **The noise and jerk move with the door** — if you watch the roller at any given panel, you can usually see it stutter or flat-spot against the track as it turns.
- **Visible wear at the roller itself**: cracked or chipped nylon, a wobbly stem, or a roller that looks oval instead of round.
- **The problem is gradual** — it got a little louder and a little rougher over months, rather than appearing suddenly after a bump or impact.

Rollers are wear items by design. In normal use (roughly 3-4 cycles a day) they typically hold up 7-10 years; heavy use, harsh weather, or a door that's been running on a misaligned track can cut that down to 5-7 years.

sections.heading: Signs it's the track
sections.body:
A bent, dented, or loosened track behaves differently — it tends to create a single, repeatable trouble spot instead of a steady noise:

- **The door jerks or jumps at the exact same point every time** — same height on the way up, same height on the way down. That repeatability is the biggest tell.
- **A visible dent, bow, or gap** where the track pulls slightly away from the roller, often where something (a car bumper, a stored ladder, a stepladder) made contact with it.
- **A loose wall bracket** — the brackets anchoring the track to the frame can work loose over time, letting the whole track flex under load.
- **It appeared suddenly**, often right after an impact, rather than building up gradually like roller wear does.

Minor dents and slight bends in an otherwise sound track can often be straightened and re-anchored. Tracks with major bends, rusted sections, or warping along a long run usually need replacement rather than repair — bending it back rarely holds under daily cycling.

sections.heading: Why ignoring either one makes both worse
sections.body: This is the part that costs people money: worn rollers and a damaged track feed each other. A roller that's gone flat or cracked doesn't roll — it scrapes, and that scraping gouges and wears the inside of the track with every cycle. A bent track does the reverse — it forces even brand-new rollers to ride at a slight angle, which chews up their bearings and nylon far faster than normal wear ever would. Run either problem long enough and you're no longer fixing one part, you're fixing both, plus whatever stress the imbalance put on the cables and opener trying to compensate for a door that won't move freely.

sections.heading: What the repair actually looks like
sections.body:
A technician diagnoses this the same way described above — running the door while watching and listening at each panel and checking the track for dents, gaps, and loose brackets — then addresses whichever part (or both) is actually failing. Roller replacement is straightforward: all rollers are replaced as a set, even if only one or two look bad, since they age together and mismatched wear throws the door out of balance again almost immediately. Track repair means re-anchoring loose brackets, straightening minor dents, and realigning the track to the door and opener's travel path; a section with major damage gets replaced outright.

This work falls in the same pricing tier as other standard cable and roller repairs: **from $150**, depending on how many rollers need replacing and whether track straightening or a track section is involved. sections.heading: What you can safely check yourself
sections.body:
You can absolutely do the diagnostic part yourself: run the door (opener disconnected if you're comfortable doing that, or just watch it run normally), and look for exactly where and how it hesitates, using the signs above. Visually inspecting rollers for cracking and tracks for dents or loose bolts is also safe with the door closed and unplugged.

Actually swapping parts is a different matter. Roller replacement is within reach for an experienced DIYer on a door that's properly balanced, but it's easy to get the track alignment wrong afterward, which just reintroduces the jerk. Track work means working near the cable and spring system that holds the door's full weight under tension — that part is not a homeowner job. If you're unsure which you're looking at, a technician can confirm it in a few minutes on-site before any repair starts.

faq.question: How can I tell if it's my rollers or my track?
faq.answer: Watch and listen to where the problem happens. A steady grinding or clicking noise on every rotation, with visible cracking or wobble at the roller itself, points to worn rollers. A jerk or jump at the exact same spot on every single cycle, especially with a visible dent or gap in the channel, points to the track. Roller wear is usually gradual; track damage often appears suddenly after an impact.

faq.question: Can I replace garage door rollers myself?
faq.answer: Experienced DIYers can often handle roller replacement on a door that's properly balanced, but getting the track alignment right afterward is easy to get wrong, which brings the jerk right back. Track repair itself works near the cable and spring system under tension and isn't a homeowner job.

faq.question: Can a bent garage door track be straightened, or does it need replacing?
faq.answer: Minor dents and slight bends can often be straightened and re-anchored successfully. Tracks with major bends, rusted sections, or warping along a long run typically need replacement — bending them back rarely holds up under daily cycling.

faq.question: What happens if I keep using the door with a bent track?
faq.answer: The problem compounds. A bent track forces even healthy rollers to ride at an angle, which wears out their bearings and nylon much faster than normal use. Left long enough, you end up needing both the track and the rollers replaced, plus extra wear on the cables and opener from the door fighting the misalignment.
